topics.title: Buenas prácticas de optimización de RAM en servidores VPS de 1GB para Node.js
topics.content: En entornos de producción con una instancia de 1 GB de RAM en la nube (AWS Lightsail / Debian 13), ¿cuáles son las configuraciones de PM2, límites de V8, pragmas de SQLite y parámetros del kernel Linux recomendados para garantizar alta disponibilidad y prevenir reinicios por Out-Of-Memory (OOM)?
topics.author: Jorge Doicela

topics.title: Best practices for RAM optimization on 1 GB VPS servers running Node.js
topics.content: In production environments operating on a strictly budgeted 1 GB RAM cloud instance (AWS Lightsail / Debian 13), what are the recommended PM2 configurations, V8 engine flags, SQLite pragmas, and Linux kernel sysctl tunings to guarantee high stability and eliminate Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes?
topics.author: Jorge Doicela

replies.author: Jorge Doicela
replies.content:
Para un VPS de 1 GB de RAM ejecutando NestJS y Next.js simultáneamente en producción sobre Debian 13, la arquitectura probada con cero caídas por OOM se fundamenta en un presupuesto de memoria estricto y 4 pilares de ingeniería:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph PhysicalRAM["Memoria RAM Física: 1024 MB (AWS Lightsail)"]
        Kernel["Kernel Linux + Nginx mTLS (~160 MB)"]
        Nest["Backend NestJS 11 (~170 MB)"]
        Next["Frontend Next.js 16 Standalone (~180 MB)"]
        WAL["SQLite WAL Cache (~25 MB)"]
        Cache["PageCache / Buffers del SO (~480 MB)"]
    end

    subgraph SwapAmortiguador["Almacenamiento NVMe Secundario"]
        Swap["Swapfile 2048 MB (vm.swappiness = 10)"]
    end

    PhysicalRAM -.->|Picos Transitorios| Swap
```

---

### 1. Contención de Heap en el Motor V8 de Node.js
Dejar que Node.js administre la memoria libremente provoca que el Garbage Collector postergue la recolección hasta superar 1.4 GB. En `pm2.config.js` se debe forzar el techo máximo mediante `--max-old-space-size`:

```javascript
// pm2.config.js - Límites de memoria y watchdog en producción
module.exports = {
  apps: [
    {
      name: 'backend-nest',
      script: './dist/main.js',
      cwd: './backend',
      node_args: '--max-old-space-size=220 --optimize-for-size',
      max_memory_restart: '250M',
      env: { NODE_ENV: 'production', PORT: 3000, HOST: '127.0.0.1' }
    },
    {
      name: 'frontend-next',
      script: './server.js',
      cwd: './frontend/web/.next/standalone/frontend/web',
      node_args: '--max-old-space-size=220 --optimize-for-size',
      max_memory_restart: '250M',
      env: { NODE_ENV: 'production', PORT: 3001, HOSTNAME: 'localhost' }
    }
  ]
};
```

---

### 2. Memoria Virtual y Swap Amortiguador en Debian 13
Un error común en VPS pequeños es deshabilitar la memoria swap. La estrategia correcta es aprovisionar un swapfile de **2 GB** en disco NVMe y reducir la agresividad de paginación a `10` en `/etc/sysctl.d/99-memory.conf`:

```ini
# Priorizar memoria RAM física antes de paginar páginas anónimas a disco
vm.swappiness = 10

# Retener inodos y directorios en caché del sistema de archivos
vm.vfs_cache_pressure = 50

# Permitir sobreasignación de memoria virtual sin pánico de kernel
vm.overcommit_memory = 1
```

```bash
# Crear swapfile de 2 GB y fijar permisos seguros
sudo fallocate -l 2G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo sysctl --system
```

---

### 3. Persistencia Ultraligera con SQLite en Modo WAL
Bases de datos cliente-servidor como PostgreSQL o MySQL consumen entre 180 MB y 300 MB en reposo únicamente por sus demonios. Con `better-sqlite3` en modo **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)**:

| Parámetro | PostgreSQL 16 | MySQL 8.0 | SQLite WAL (better-sqlite3) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Consumo Base RAM** | ~220 MB | ~280 MB | **~15 - 25 MB** |
| **Proceso de Ejecución** | Demonio Separado | Demonio Separado | **In-Process (Mismo proceso Node.js)** |
| **Límite de WAL** | Rotación compleja | Logs binarios pesados | **`PRAGMA journal_size_limit = 67108864;` (64 MB)** |
| **Viabilidad en 1 GB RAM** | Inviable (Riesgo OOM) | Inviable (Riesgo OOM) | **Óptimo (Estabilidad absoluta)** |

```sql
-- Pragmas de alto rendimiento y bajo consumo aplicados en cada módulo
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;
PRAGMA journal_size_limit = 67108864;
PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;
PRAGMA cache_size = -20000; -- 20 MB de caché en RAM
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;
```

---

### 4. Conclusión y Telemetría Observada
Con esta arquitectura, el consumo medio de RAM en producción se mantiene en **~520 MB de 1024 MB (51% de ocupación)**, dejando más de **450 MB de margen libre** para picos de tráfico, compilaciones de mantenimiento y cachés del sistema operativo sin experimentar reinicios no planificados.

replies.author: Jorge Doicela
replies.content:
For a 1 GB RAM VPS running both NestJS and Next.js concurrently on Debian 13, our production-validated architecture achieving zero OOM crashes is built on a disciplined memory budget and 4 engineering pillars:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph PhysicalRAM["Physical Hardware RAM: 1024 MB (AWS Lightsail)"]
        Kernel["Linux Kernel + Nginx mTLS (~160 MB)"]
        Nest["NestJS 11 Backend (~170 MB)"]
        Next["Next.js 16 Standalone (~180 MB)"]
        WAL["SQLite WAL Cache (~25 MB)"]
        Cache["OS PageCache / Buffers (~480 MB)"]
    end

    subgraph SwapBuffer["Secondary NVMe Storage"]
        Swap["2048 MB Swapfile (vm.swappiness = 10)"]
    end

    PhysicalRAM -.->|Transient Spikes| Swap
```

---

### 1. Heap Containment inside Node.js V8 Engine
Leaving Node.js unconstrained allows its generational garbage collector to postpone full compaction cycles until memory usage crosses 1.4 GB. In `pm2.config.js`, cap heap growth via `--max-old-space-size`:

```javascript
// pm2.config.js - Production memory bounds and watchdog
module.exports = {
  apps: [
    {
      name: 'backend-nest',
      script: './dist/main.js',
      cwd: './backend',
      node_args: '--max-old-space-size=220 --optimize-for-size',
      max_memory_restart: '250M',
      env: { NODE_ENV: 'production', PORT: 3000, HOST: '127.0.0.1' }
    },
    {
      name: 'frontend-next',
      script: './server.js',
      cwd: './frontend/web/.next/standalone/frontend/web',
      node_args: '--max-old-space-size=220 --optimize-for-size',
      max_memory_restart: '250M',
      env: { NODE_ENV: 'production', PORT: 3001, HOSTNAME: 'localhost' }
    }
  ]
};
```

---

### 2. Virtual Memory and Buffer Swapfile on Debian 13
A common anti-pattern on small VPS instances is disabling swap entirely. The correct strategy is allocating a **2 GB** NVMe swapfile and dampening swap aggressiveness to `10` in `/etc/sysctl.d/99-memory.conf`:

```ini
# Prioritize physical RAM before paging anonymous memory to NVMe
vm.swappiness = 10

# Maintain dentries and filesystem inodes in kernel cache
vm.vfs_cache_pressure = 50

# Allow virtual memory overcommit without kernel panic
vm.overcommit_memory = 1
```

```bash
# Allocate 2 GB swapfile with strict permissions
sudo fallocate -l 2G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo sysctl --system
```

---

### 3. Ultra-lean Persistence with SQLite in WAL Mode
Client-server relational engines like PostgreSQL or MySQL demand 180 MB to 300 MB of baseline RAM purely for their background daemons. By employing `better-sqlite3` in **Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** mode:

| Metric | PostgreSQL 16 | MySQL 8.0 | SQLite WAL (better-sqlite3) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Baseline RAM** | ~220 MB | ~280 MB | **~15 - 25 MB** |
| **Execution Model** | Standalone Daemon | Standalone Daemon | **In-Process (Embedded in Node.js)** |
| **WAL Ceiling** | Heavy binary logs | Complex tablespaces | **`PRAGMA journal_size_limit = 67108864;` (64 MB)** |
| **1 GB VPS Viability** | Unviable (OOM Risk) | Unviable (OOM Risk) | **Optimal (Rock-solid Stability)** |

```sql
-- High-throughput, memory-bounded pragmas applied per module connection
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;
PRAGMA journal_size_limit = 67108864;
PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;
PRAGMA cache_size = -20000; -- 20 MB RAM cache
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;
```

---

### 4. Conclusion and Observed Telemetry
Under this architecture, median production RAM consumption holds at **~520 MB out of 1024 MB (51% utilization)**, preserving over **450 MB of headroom** for sudden traffic surges, maintenance tasks, and OS buffer caches with zero unplanned service recycles.
